entries.text: The Perl IDE Survey provides community driven insights into tools, editors, and workflows. It shows the preferred main choices such as Vim and VS Code and metrics on LSP, testing practices, and other main programming tools.
entries.title: Perl IDE Developer Survey 2026

entries.author: ron_savage
entries.text: Ron Savage has announced the availability of Perl.Wiki (version 1.56), as well as CPAN::MetaCurator (version 1.33). This new version integrates ChangeLog features into the JSTree menu and also improves the overall appearance of the program's interface.
entries.title: ANNOUNCE: Perl.Wiki V 1.56, CPAN::MetaCurator V 1.33

entries.author: olaf_alders
entries.text: CPAN authors are reminded by Olaf Alders to stop using their @cpan.org email accounts permanently after the Perl NOC closed the forwarding service earlier this year. The maintenance of correct MetaCPAN profiles and contact information enables the CPAN Security Group to get in touch with maintainers regarding urgent security notifications.
entries.title: It's Time to Retire Your @cpan.org Email Address

entries.author: andrew_speer
entries.text: Andrew has presented a novel set of CPAN modules made to connect the latest Markdown and DocBook process with traditional Perl POD. The article underscores the sidecar markdown documentation files that get automatically integrated with source files thanks to MakeMaker's goals together with the software for making rich and static sites.
entries.title: Perl documentation (including POD) with Markdown and Docbook

entries.text: In the most recent update from the Perl Steering Council (Issue #238), discussions regarding the improvement of @INC handling continue. They also provide an update on the results of monitoring the effects of changes made to the way anonymous subroutines generate line numbers.
entries.title: This week in PSC (238) | 2026-10-05

entries.author: dani_otelch
entries.text: Dani describes how the Minion framework, which is part of Mojolicious, supports background job processing and SQL data storage in Perl applications. This article presents a detailed explanation and proposes Minion as a simpler and better option than heavy queue-based systems using Redis or kinds of enterprise-level job queues.
entries.title: Minion: The Silent Engine That Turns Perl Into a Modern Architecture Platform

entries.author: petamem
entries.text: PetaMem showcases Peta::NN, a zero-dependency neural networking library created from Perl, which can build and train micro-models such as inflection and word category. The post also describes things like modular pipelines, GPU acceleration (using Peta::WebGPU), and tested apps (like accurate German noun pluralisation).
entries.title: Peta::NN - Surface Detail

entries.author: robert_acock
entries.text: Robert presents Game::Terminal, a single consolidated CPAN distribution of over twenty terminal-based classic board, card, and arcade games. The post explains how a clean and modular engine design powers both this new CLI menu launcher and an upcoming browser-based gaming platform.
entries.title: Game::Terminal: Perl game implementations in a terminal

entries.author: dave_cross
entries.text: Dave makes observations regarding the history of Perl for 24 years and looks at the history and origins of the URL shortening module suite WWW::Shorten after making corrections since some of the email addresses from that period are now retired.
entries.title: The Long Life of WWW::Shorten

entries.author: mohammad_anwar
entries.text: Welcome to a new week with a couple of fun tasks "Complex Number" and "Word Squares". If you are new to the weekly challenge then why not join us and have fun every week. For more information, please read the FAQ.
entries.title: The Weekly Challenge - 395

entries.author: mohammad_anwar
entries.text: Enjoy a quick recap of last week's contributions by Team PWC dealing with the "Alternate Case" and "Alternating Vowels Consonants" tasks in Perl and Raku. You will find plenty of solutions to keep you busy.
entries.title: RECAP - The Weekly Challenge - 394

entries.author: jorg_sommrey
entries.text: The article provides a neat solution to the problems of case-alternation and vowel-consonant sequencers through the use of two languages (Perl and J) represented in one beautiful algorithm. Jorg successfully illustrates the advanced features for controlling the pattern-matching process such as (*MARK) and (*SKIP), which lead to the elimination of unnecessary backtracking.
entries.title: Regular Alternations

entries.author: lubos_kolouch
entries.text: This multilingual blog post (in Perl and Python) presents solutions that are simple and well-documented and efficiently mix the techniques of ingenious index matching for the first task with the techniques of effective substring reduction for the second task. The code is simple, easy to read, and demonstrates good algorithms at every step.
entries.title: The Weekly Challenge #394

entries.author: luis_mochan
entries.text: The blog entry written by Luis Mochan contains useful and very clear Perl-centric coverage of Challenge 394. In tackling Task 1, he makes use of creative combination of character and bit swapping (transforming the cases into binary digits), while for Task 2, he employs an aesthetically pleasing method of filtering fragments / finding the longest string.
entries.title: Perl Weekly Challenge 394

entries.author: packy_anderson
entries.text: Packy's article offers an interesting and informative piece in multiple languages, including Raku, Perl, Python, and Elixir. The article is based on Yes's Tales from Topographic Oceans and discusses some innovative methods of how one can solve problems of case-changing and finding subsequences with the use of regex.
entries.title: Alternate Tune, Alternate View

entries.author: peter_campbell_smith
entries.text: The Perl approach employs a straightforward greedy scan-and-shift method along with a two-pass check (the original string and with the first two characters interchanged) to arrive at the minimum number of adjacent swaps. The approach is compact and well-documented and provides a thorough overview of the heuristics employed in the process.
entries.title: Alternation week

entries.author: robbie_hatley
entries.text: Robbie's Perl solutions demonstrate clever structural reasoning with the help of simple positional cost calculation for switching cases along with structured bitmask/sorting hash for discovering longest alternating vowel-consonants substrings.
entries.title: The Weekly Challenge #394

entries.author: roger_bell_west
entries.text: In his blog, Roger presents a sophisticated technical explanation of the solution to The Weekly Challenge 394 in Perl and Crystal. Task 1 utilises an ingenious breadth-first search on case-state configuration, while Task 2 creates a modular solution through separating the substring extraction and the logic of alternation in a vowel-consonant manner.
entries.title: Alternating Everything

entries.author: simon_green
entries.text: Simon's blog has come up with a cleanly written solution to the Weekly Challenge 394 problem in Python. In addition, the blog post illustrates Simon's input validation techniques followed by some easy to understand helper functions.
entries.title: The one about alternating

header: The combination of artificial intelligence and automatic tooling in open source software maintenance has emerged as a common trend throughout modern development ecosystems, including CPAN. Writers and maintainers are experimenting with various ways of work, ranging from the use of generative AI for quick patch creation and refactoring to the creation of development tools that interact with external language models. These innovations point out to a wider trend in the industry aimed at incorporating AI features into typical software life cycles and source code maintenance processes.

Advocates of AI based development stress major benefits associated with maintainability, speed of work, and solving problems, particularly in the context of outdated programs. Thanks to automation of repetitive processes handled by AI or code-generating programs, the developer team would be able to fix errors, create documentation easier, and minimise routine labour costs.

Unsupervised machine-generated codes bring along the chances of bug occurrences, the chances of APIs not existing and the issues related to licensing laws. With AI tools incorporated in the software distribution processes, open source communities are obliged to deal with serious issues of code quality, sustainability and the important line of distinction between machine generated and human generated codes.

With the growth in the use of AI assisted contributions, open source communities are facing the challenge of review fatigue and diminishing basic trust. In the absence of established rules on disclosure and human verification, maintainers have to devote more time to scrutinise incoming code to detect any secret problems.

In spite of the changes in debates, the ongoing runs of new distributions in CPAN are evidence of the incredible allegiance of the Perl community. Every contribution, ranging from tools upgrades to improving basic utilities, is contributing to strengthening the environment used by developers from all over the globe.
subject: Perl and AI
